promptText: What core Java/Spring concept is Spring AI's Advisor abstraction architecturally most similar to?
options: Java's equals()/hashCode() contract
Servlet filters / Spring AOP around-advice, offering composable, ordered interception with the ability to short-circuit
The Builder design pattern for object construction
JPA entity lifecycle callbacks
explanation: Advisors deliberately reuse the interceptor/Chain-of-Responsibility mental model from servlet Filters and Spring AOP's around-advice, wrapping a core call with composable, ordered, independent behavior.

promptText: In a ChatClient advisor chain, does any individual advisor call the model provider directly?
options: Yes, every advisor makes its own separate call to the model
No -- advisors wrap 'the rest of the chain,' and the actual model call happens once, in a terminal step at the end of the chain
Only the first advisor in the chain calls the model
Only advisors marked @Primary can call the model
explanation: No advisor calls the model directly; each one decides whether to invoke the rest of the chain, and the framework's terminal step is the only place the actual network call to the model happens.

promptText: What does it mean for an advisor to 'short-circuit' the chain?
options: It caches the model's response for reuse on the next identical request
It decides not to invoke the rest of the chain and returns a response directly, so no advisor further down (nor the model) is ever invoked
It runs two advisors in parallel instead of sequentially
It converts a blocking call into a streaming one
explanation: Short-circuiting is how a safety advisor can reject a request before it ever reaches the model, skipping every downstream advisor and paying zero tokens and latency for a call that would have been discarded.

promptText: What determines the relative order in which registered advisors execute, if no explicit order is set?
options: Alphabetical order of each advisor's class name
Registration order, which is fragile since it depends on the sequence advisors happened to be added to the builder
Advisors execute in a random order chosen per request for load balancing
The order is always determined by declared field order in the @Configuration class
explanation: Without explicit order values the framework falls back to registration order, which is easy to get wrong as advisors are added over time by different people; explicit ordering is the recommended practice.

promptText: Which built-in Spring AI advisor performs the retrieval-augmentation step of RAG by querying a vector store and injecting matching documents into the prompt?
options: SimpleLoggerAdvisor
SafeGuardAdvisor
QuestionAnswerAdvisor
MessageChatMemoryAdvisor
explanation: QuestionAnswerAdvisor is the standard RAG advisor: on the way in, it runs a similarity search against a configured vector store and rewrites the prompt to include retrieved context.

promptText: On the response side, in what order do advisors process the model's reply as it flows back to the caller?
options: The exact same order they processed the request on the way in
The exact reverse order -- the last advisor to touch the outgoing request is the first to see the raw response
A newly randomized order for each response
Only advisors marked as 'response-aware' process the reply at all
explanation: The response travels back up through the chain in exact reverse order, mirroring how code after chain.doFilter(...) in a servlet filter runs on the way back out.

promptText: Why does Spring AI define separate advisor contracts for blocking calls versus streaming calls, instead of one universal interface?
options: Streaming requires a completely different network protocol that advisors can't intercept
A blocking call produces one response object an advisor can inspect synchronously, while a streaming call produces a Flux of partial chunks over time that must be buffered or transformed differently
Spring AI doesn't actually support advisors on streaming calls
Blocking advisors run on a different thread pool than streaming advisors
explanation: Wrapping a single response object and wrapping a reactive Flux of partial chunks genuinely require different code, so Spring AI's Advisor API treats both call shapes as first-class from the start.

promptText: A team chains a RAG advisor and a safety/guardrail advisor. If the safety advisor runs before the RAG advisor and only inspects the user's literal typed message, what risk does this create?
options: None -- the RAG advisor never modifies message content the safety check would need
It misses injected instructions hidden inside documents the RAG advisor later appends, since those are combined with the request only after the safety check already ran
It causes a compile-time error because advisor order must always put safety first
It doubles the token cost of every request
explanation: A safety check scoped only to the user's literal message and positioned before retrieval never sees injected instructions hidden inside retrieved document content, a well-documented RAG attack surface.

promptText: What is the purpose of the shared, request-scoped 'advisor context' that travels through the chain?
options: It stores the model provider's API key securely for each advisor to use
It lets independent advisors coordinate (e.g., one advisor stashes a conversation ID that another reads) without either one depending on the other's class
It caches the final response so future identical requests skip the chain entirely
It is the mechanism used to enforce advisor execution order
explanation: The shared context map is the same idea as a servlet request's attribute map: it lets advisors that don't know about each other's implementation coordinate through a common key-value structure.

promptText: Why is placing a PII-redaction advisor before both a logging advisor and a memory advisor important?
options: Redaction is computationally expensive and should run last to avoid slowing down the chain
If redaction ran after logging, the raw PII would already have been written to logs regardless of what redaction does afterward -- the leak already happened
Logging advisors automatically redact PII themselves, making order irrelevant
Memory advisors cannot process redacted text
explanation: Ordering determines what data downstream advisors can see; redaction running early ensures logging and memory only ever observe the redacted version, never the raw sensitive input.

promptText: What is the risk of implementing memory, logging, retrieval, and safety all inside one large 'MasterAdvisor' class instead of separate advisors?
options: Spring AI technically forbids registering more than one advisor per ChatClient
It becomes impossible to independently reorder, test, reuse, or selectively disable any one concern without risking regressions in the others
A single advisor class cannot access the shared advisor context
It would double the latency of every request compared to separate advisors
explanation: Independent concerns should be independent advisors composed via ordering; a monolithic advisor loses the ability to reorder, test, or reuse concerns separately, and an edit for one concern risks regressing another.

promptText: A caching advisor computes its cache key only from the literal prompt text, and a per-user memory advisor also sits in the same chain. What subtle bug can result?
options: The cache key becomes too large to store efficiently

Two different users who phrase a question identically could receive a cached response generated in the context of someone else's injected conversation history -- a cross-user data leak through the cache
The memory advisor will throw a NullPointerException whenever caching is enabled
Advisors cannot coexist with caching at all in Spring AI
explanation: If the cache key doesn't include the identity/conversation dimension memory depends on, a cached response generated with one user's history can leak to another user asking a similarly-worded question.

promptText: In an advisor chain with a rate limiter, PII redaction, conversation memory, RAG retrieval, and a safety check, why does it make sense to run the safety check after memory and RAG rather than immediately after redaction?
options: Safety checks are always required to run first, before any other advisor, as a hard framework constraint

The safety check should evaluate the complete assembled request -- history plus retrieved context plus the new message -- since that combined payload, not just the raw new message, is the actual content reaching the model
Running safety checks late reduces their computational cost by batching them with the model call
Memory and RAG advisors are required to run before any advisor that can short-circuit the chain
explanation: Safety evaluated after history and retrieval have been assembled inspects the actual attack surface being sent to the model, rather than only the newest, isolated user message.

promptText: Why does adding several advisors to a high-QPS chat endpoint sometimes measurably hurt p99 (tail) latency, even when each advisor is fast on average?
options: Advisors execute on a single shared thread that becomes a bottleneck under any load

The probability that at least one advisor experiences a slow outlier (GC pause, slow store response) on a given call rises with the number of advisors, and end-to-end p99 reflects the slowest link on that call, not the average across all of them
Spring AI serializes all advisor execution across a global lock regardless of chain length
Each additional advisor doubles the number of network calls to the model provider
explanation: Tail latencies compose worse than averages: with more advisors in the chain, the chance that at least one is slow on any given call rises, and p99 reflects whichever link was slowest on that call.

promptText: A production incident shows one user occasionally receiving another user's prior conversation turns in their responses. Using advisor concepts, what is the most likely root cause?
options: The Advisor chain mechanism itself leaks shared context between unrelated concurrent requests by design

The memory advisor's conversation ID is derived from something not actually unique per user/session, or a stateful instance field on the advisor is being reused across concurrent requests instead of per-call context
The model provider is caching responses server-side across different customers
The logging advisor is misconfigured to print other users' data
explanation: Advisors are meant to be stateless singletons; the near-universal cause of cross-user history bleed is a conversation-id scoping bug or a stateful field on the advisor being reused across concurrent requests.
